paper_style.palette_strategy: Figure 1 uses orange/blue/light-green dataset bars and black average line; Figures 2/3/6 use saturated normal/error pseudo-colors; Figure 4 uses yellow lights and orange rays; Figure 5 uses blue/orange/green branches and status icons; Tables 1–6 use black rules with pale-green/pale-blue best/second-best cells. No single palette has one semantic meaning across all objects.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Tables 1–6, captions, body text and some labels/rules are PDF objects; Figure 1 is assembled from many raster panels plus a 7200×1800 chart raster, Figure 2 from many JPEG panels, Figure 3 from a 1595×797 raster, Figure 4 from a 1466×967 transparent raster plus labels, Figure 5 from a 6342×1233 raster, and Figure 6 from a 4430×2884 raster. Only the Figure 1 rendered teaser is publicly available as a visual asset, not editable source.
paper_style.style_consistency: Letter page geometry, caption placement, Method/Mean table structure, metric arrows and best/second-best highlighting are stable. Figure families use different local grammars, while 5–14 pt raster labels, high-density tables, pseudo-color dependence, missing uncertainty, and absent appendix material are repeated limitations.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: We present RoSE, a method using a video generative model for monocular normal map estimation, built on a new paradigm that reformulates normal estimation as a shading sequence estimation task. Results on complex and diverse scenarios show that RoSE reconstructs fine-grained geometric details and generalizes robustly to unseen datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in object-based monocular normal estimation on benchmark datasets.

color.semantic_mapping: LUCES/DiLiGenT/MultiShade bars, black Average line, red Ours value, and RGB normal-map directions; labels and grouping provide partial redundancy.

encodings.text: method names, bar values, and caption

figures.data_and_statistics: The lower chart aggregates LUCES, DiLiGenT, and MultiShade mean angular error for GeoWizard, DSINE, StableNormal, Lotus-D, Lotus-G, Neural LightRig, NiRNE, and Ours; the Average line gives the three-dataset mean (Ours 15.40). The upper two rows are representative normal-map comparisons, not a sample statistic; no error bars, repeats, denominators, or failures are shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduction headline connects the visible 3D-misalignment problem to the shading-sequence proposal; Tables 1–3 expand the chart means and Figures 2/6 provide local qualitative evidence.
design_strengths: Combines representative qualitative evidence and the cross-dataset headline in one page-width visual.
Aligned method columns and a red Ours average make the primary comparison immediately scannable.
design_weaknesses: High information density mixes natural images, normal maps, bars, a line, and caption claims.
No uncertainty or aggregation annotation; only two qualitative objects are shown and pseudo-colors are not grayscale-safe.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a fixed method-column montage above a grouped-bar chart with a single average line, but annotate aggregation, repeats, uncertainty, and the normal/error color semantics.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Illustration of 3D misalignment. The estimated normal maps of previous methods may appear to have an overall correct appearance, yet the reconstructed surfaces often fail to align with the accurate geometry details, showing over-smooth results. In contrast, our predicted normal maps exhibit better 3D alignment, leading to more faithful surface reconstruction.

color.semantic_mapping: RGB normal-map direction, grayscale surface reconstruction, red crop/arrow, and blue surface border; column/row labels provide textual redundancy.

encodings.color: RGB normal direction versus grayscale geometry; crop and border colors

figures.data_and_statistics: Six columns compare StableNormal, Neural LightRig, GeoWizard, NiRNE, Ours, and Ground Truth on one teapot. The upper normal maps have red flower-detail boxes, middle crops enlarge that detail, and lower grayscale surfaces show reconstruction; there are no numerical metrics, repeats, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: The Introduction claim that normal maps can look right while surfaces are 3D-misaligned is made visible; Figure 3 then quantifies representation sensitivity and §3 supplies the shading/OLS bridge.
design_strengths: Same object, crop, and column geometry make appearance and reconstructed-surface mismatch directly comparable.
The crop arrow turns the abstract fine-detail claim into a localized visual test.
design_weaknesses: One teapot cannot establish population-level alignment; no error metric accompanies the surface row.
RGB normal-map semantics and crop/surface border colors are not colorblind or grayscale robust, and six columns are small at page scale.
figures.reusable_pattern: For dense prediction tasks, align full prediction, fixed local crop, and reconstructed geometry in one method-column grid; pair it with a rule for selecting representative units and aggregate error.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Validation of sensitivity to geometry variations for different representations, including the proposed shading sequence (left) and the normal map (right), measured by average total variation (TV). TV is computed as the mean magnitude of the first-order image’s gradient in terms of different representations, where higher TV indicates stronger sensitivity to spatial geometric variation.

color.semantic_mapping: Shared blue-to-red pseudo-color depicts local gradient/sensitivity; left Shading and right Normal panels report TV=0.66 and 0.14.

figures.data_and_statistics: A 1595 × 797 raster comparison shows the same teapot under Shading and Normal representations. Average total variation is 0.66 for shading and 0.14 for normal; the caption defines TV as mean first-order gradient magnitude. No object count, seed, repeated measurement, or uncertainty is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 2 motivates the 3D-alignment problem; this image-level diagnostic supports the claim that shading sequences expose geometry variation more strongly, which is formalized by Eqs. (1)–(4) and used by Figure 5.
design_strengths: Shared object and TV values make the representation contrast concise.
A color scale and numeric TV annotations connect visual texture to an explicit diagnostic.
design_weaknesses: Colorbar has no numeric tick scale or normalization; one case and one point estimate cannot establish general sensitivity.
Small inset and pseudo-color limit precise reading and grayscale accessibility.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show original and proposed intermediate representations side by side with one sensitivity metric, while adding sample scope, normalization, replicates, and a readable scale.

figures.label: Figure 4

color.semantic_mapping: Yellow glyphs are canonical parallel lights, orange dashed rays show directions, red center marks object/reference, and the lamp image supplies a physical example.

encodings.line: dashed light rays and center line

figures.data_and_statistics: The diagram shows a lamp/object at left and six yellow light glyphs distributed on an upper-hemisphere ring, with orange dashed rays to a central red point. It is a physical design schematic, not a performance statistic; the figure omits latitude, distance, intensity, and uncertainty. The text uses the six-light construction for Lemma 1 but reports nine lights as the empirical best.
figures.evidence_relation: Eq. (4) full-rank recovery and Lemma 1 motivate the ring geometry; §3.2 then chooses the light count and Table 6 tests a spiral alternative.
design_strengths: Separates the object and canonical-light geometry clearly.
Icons and dashed rays give an immediate spatial explanation of positive-light coverage.
design_weaknesses: Six displayed lights can be confused with the experimental nine-light default.
No coordinate system, 45° latitude, intensity, scale, or explicit l_min annotation is provided.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a physical object photo with normalized light glyphs, but label theoretical lower bound and experimental default separately.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Pipeline of RoSE. Given a monocular RGB image under arbitrary light, RoSE first converts it into a grayscale image, which is then used to generate the shading sequence via a video diffusion model. This generation is guided by two complementary feature representations extracted from a CLIP encoder and a VAE encoder. Finally, an ordinary least squares problem is solved analytically to estimate the normal map from the generated shading sequence. We train the video diffusion model while freezing the CLIP and the VAE encoder.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue CLIP/global branch, orange VAE/local branch, green video diffusion, yellow parallel lights, black locks/arrows, and white/gray outputs; lock/flame/light icons redundantly encode training status and physics.

encodings.color: conditioning branch/module role and light status
encodings.line: solid arrows and dashed module boundaries

figures.data_and_statistics: A 6342 × 1233 raster pipeline maps RGB Image → Grayscale Conversion → Gray Image → CLIP/VAE dual conditioning → Video Diffusion Model → Predicted Shading Sequence under canonical lights → Analytic Solver → Predicted Normal. It encodes no sample or performance statistic; the lock/flame legend marks frozen versus trainable components.
figures.evidence_relation: Eqs. (3)–(5) define the grayscale-to-shading-to-normal bridge and diffusion objective; this figure makes that method interface explicit before Tables 4–5 and Table 6 test intermediate quality and variants.
design_strengths: The single flow exposes intermediate representation, analytic inverse, frozen encoders, and trainable generator.
Color-coded dual conditioning and a compact legend make implementation boundaries reusable.
design_weaknesses: Tensor shapes, diffusion timestep/loss route, light count, compute cost, and failure path are omitted.
Rasterized labels soften on enlargement and no editable public diagram source is available.
figures.reusable_pattern: For a generated-intermediate-plus-analytic-solver method, draw input, conditioners, generator, intermediate, solver, output, and one shared freeze/train/physics legend.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on selected objects from two benchmark dataset (COW from DiLiGenT (Shi et al., 2016) and SQUIRREL from LUCES (Mecca et al., 2021). Row 1 & 3: normal map comparison. Row 2 & 4: error map comparison.) Best viewed in color with zooming in.

color.semantic_mapping: Normal maps use saturated direction colors, error maps use a shared 0°–50° blue-to-red angular-error scale, and GT/Ref RGB retain natural colors; MAE numbers provide limited redundancy.

figures.data_and_statistics: A 4430 × 2884 raster grid has nine columns: GT Normal/Ref RGB, GeoWizard, DSINE, StableNormal, Lotus-G, Lotus-D, Neural LightRig, NiRNE, and Ours. Four rows show Cow normal/error and Squirrel normal/error; error values include Cow Ours=13.28 and Squirrel Ours=21.34, with a shared 0°–50° colorbar. These are selected objects, without selection rule, repeats, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Tables 1–2 give benchmark means; Figure 6 localizes the fine-detail/artifact claim on Cow (DiLiGenT) and Squirrel (LUCES), while Table 5 supplies the boundary SNE diagnostic.
design_strengths: Aligned GT/input, predictions, errors, and MAE make method differences visually immediate.
A shared error colorbar maintains a common angular-error scale across objects and methods.
design_weaknesses: Thirty-six dense cells and small labels require zooming; RGB normal/error colors are not grayscale-safe.
Two selected objects cannot establish benchmark-wide robustness and no uncertainty or selection rule is shown.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a fixed method-column qualitative grid with normal/error rows and one shared error scale, then report how objects were selected and pair it with full-population uncertainty.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Quantitative comparison in terms of MAE (↓) of the normal map on DiLiGenT benchmark dataset. Highlighted numbers indicate the best and second best results among monocular estimation methods.

tables.uncertainty: Each object value is averaged across the selected 10 images and the Mean averages objects; no SD/SE, interval, seed spread, or failure count is reported.
tables.data_and_statistics: DiLiGenT object-level and mean normal-map MAE (degrees, lower is better) for eight methods: GeoWizard, DSINE, StableNormal, Lotus-D, Lotus-G, Neural LightRig, NiRNE, and Ours.
tables.evidence_relation: The §4.1–4.2 MAE protocol feeds the distant/parallel-light benchmark table; its Mean is one component of Figure 1 and its object-level exceptions motivate Figure 6/Table 5.
design_strengths: Per-object columns retain heterogeneity next to the aggregate Mean.
Green/blue best and second-best highlighting is fast to scan.
design_weaknesses: Twelve columns and ~7 pt text are dense.
Point means hide image-level variation and caption omits the selected-image rule.
tables.reusable_pattern: Keep a stable per-object benchmark order and report Mean beside units, with selection and uncertainty metadata.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Quantitative comparison in terms of MAE of the normal map on LUCES benchmark dataset (Mecca et al., 2021). Highlighted numbers indicate the best and second best results among monocular estimation methods.

tables.uncertainty: Each object value is averaged across the selected 10 images and Mean averages objects; no SD/SE, repeated-seed spread, interval, failure, or cost is reported.
tables.data_and_statistics: LUCES near-field object-level and mean normal-map MAE (degrees, lower is better) over 14 objects and eight methods; Ours Mean=14.48 and Lotus-G Mean=17.44, while Ours House=36.79 is a local exception.
tables.evidence_relation: Extends Table 1 from distant to near-field lighting; Figure 1 combines its Mean with Tables 1 and 3, while Table 5 and Table 6 inspect detail and causal components.
design_strengths: Fourteen objects expose heterogeneity in near-field generalization.
The same Method+objects+Mean structure makes cross-benchmark comparison easy.
design_weaknesses: Sixteen columns are difficult to read at page scale.
No object distribution or uncertainty accompanies the aggregate and caption omits sampling details.
tables.reusable_pattern: Reuse a per-unit table across physical regimes and surface exceptional units rather than only the Mean.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: Quantitative comparison in terms of Mean and Median Angular Errors of the normal map on MultiShade test set, and the percentage of objects below a specific error bound. Highlighted numbers indicate the best and second best results among monocular estimation methods.

tables.uncertainty: Point estimates only: no seed spread, interval, or sampling uncertainty. The body states 100 unseen objects and 2,800 samples, while the caption calls the threshold percentages percentages of objects; the exact object/sample aggregation denominator is not specified.
tables.data_and_statistics: MultiShade mean and median angular error plus percentages below 3°, 5°, 7.5°, 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° thresholds for eight methods. Ours is 15.37 mean, 7.78 median, and 26.99/38.38/49.00/60.32/78.30/84.28% coverage.
tables.evidence_relation: The unseen-material/light experiment extends Tables 1–2; threshold coverage feeds Figure 1’s MultiShade bar and Figure 6’s representative error maps.
design_strengths: Mean, median, and multiple threshold coverages share one decision surface.
Metric arrows and cell highlights clarify direction and local bests.
design_weaknesses: Objects versus 2,800 samples is not a closed denominator.
No coverage uncertainty or tie policy is shown, and the compact table is small.
tables.reusable_pattern: Place aggregate error, median, and preregistered threshold coverage together while making the unit of aggregation explicit.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4: Quantitative comparison on estimated shading sequence in terms of PSNR (↑), SSIM (↑), and LPIPS (↓) on LUCES benchmark dataset (Mecca et al., 2021). Highlighted numbers indicate the best and second best results.

tables.uncertainty: No repeats, dispersion, confidence interval, frame count, or uncertainty is reported. PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS are point metrics.
tables.data_and_statistics: LUCES estimated shading-sequence comparison: PSNR and SSIM higher is better, LPIPS lower is better; Ours=20.74/0.7744/0.2583. Other methods’ shading maps, including ground truth, are computed from light-direction/normal dot products with negative values clamped to zero.
tables.evidence_relation: Tests the intermediate output of Figure 5 and the representation claim in Figure 3 before final normal MAE in Tables 1–2; it is not an independent causal intervention because baselines are post-derived.
design_strengths: Compact metric-first header makes three intermediate-output metrics easy to compare.
Best/second-best fills align with the rest of the results tables.
design_weaknesses: Baseline shading is constructed from predicted normals rather than a common direct sequence predictor.
Mixed 2/4 decimal precision and no uncertainty hinder exact comparison.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report intermediate fidelity beside final-task error and distinguish direct predictions from derived baseline quantities.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Quantitative analysis in terms of MAE and SNE of the normal map on LUCES benchmark dataset (Mecca et al., 2021). Highlighted numbers indicate the best and second best results.

tables.uncertainty: Point estimates only; no boundary-pixel/object count, repeat, SD/SE, interval, or uncertainty is given.
tables.data_and_statistics: LUCES normal-map MAE and boundary-region Sharp Normal Error (SNE), both lower-is-better angular errors. Ours=14.48/26.74 and NiRNE=17.88/26.78.
tables.evidence_relation: Connects Figure 2/6’s fine-detail alignment claim to a boundary metric and complements Table 6’s mechanism ablations.
design_strengths: Overall MAE and boundary SNE expose different aspects of detail alignment in one small table.
Minimal header makes the closest SNE comparison visible.
design_weaknesses: SNE region construction and denominator are not quantified.
“Comparable” detail performance is unsupported by uncertainty or full-object distributions.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair a global metric with a prespecified boundary/detail metric and publish its region definition and uncertainty.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Ablation study in terms of MAE of the normal map on LUCES benchmark dataset (Mecca et al., 2021). In particular, “+M”(“+L”) means training on Multishade (LightProp) dataset, ‘w/o clamp’ means removing clamping on shading sequence. ‘w/o MA’ means training on dataset without material augmentation. Highlighted numbers indicate the best and second best results.

tables.uncertainty: All entries are point MAE estimates; no matched-budget statement, seed spread, SD/SE, interval, training cost, or failure value is included.
tables.data_and_statistics: LUCES object-level and mean MAE across 10 rows: Lotus-G, Neural LightRig, Ours w/o clamp, Ours w/o MA, Lotus-G+M, Ours+L, Ours w/ spiral, Ours w/ RGB, Ours w/ SVD XL, and Ours. Variants isolate clamp, material augmentation, dataset, backbone, grayscale input, and ring-light path; Ours Mean=14.48, w/o clamp=15.88, w/o MA=16.19, Ours+L=15.21, spiral=17.60, RGB=15.27, SVD XL=14.58.
tables.evidence_relation: Returns from Figure 5/Eqs. (1)–(5) to component, data, backbone, input, and light-path interventions; it is the final main-paper evidence after Tables 1–5.
design_strengths: Per-object columns expose where variants help or hurt rather than only reporting Mean.
Several independent design choices are placed on one comparable LUCES surface.
design_weaknesses: Multiple variants are not fully matched causal interventions and budgets are absent.
Ten rows × sixteen columns are dense; local reversals such as House require prose interpretation.
tables.reusable_pattern: For multi-factor ablations, keep a fixed per-unit table, identify the primary contrast for every row, and add budget/effect/uncertainty summaries.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 establishes the headline; Figure 2 makes 3D misalignment visible; Figure 3 gives the shading-versus-normal sensitivity bridge; Figure 4 fixes ring-light geometry; Figure 5 explains the grayscale→video diffusion→shading→OLS pipeline; Tables 1–3 provide benchmark and MultiShade outcomes; Figure 6 and Tables 4–5 connect outcomes to local error, intermediate sequence quality and boundary detail; Table 6 decomposes implementation/data/path choices; Discussion states compute, lighting, material and object-centric limits.
cross_object_system.caption_system: All captions use Figure/Table number followed by title and, where available, setup/encoding. Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 5 state a main finding; Figure 4 is only a title; most result tables describe metrics and highlighting without values or uncertainty. No caption supplies complete seed, denominator and selection information.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Tables 1, 2 and 6 share Method + per-object + Mean; Tables 3–5 use compact metric-first headers. MAE/PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS arrows indicate direction, while pale green/blue fills and bold mark best/second-best; tie and aggregation policies are unstated.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Eqs. (1)–(5), Figure 3 and Figure 5 define the intermediate shading representation and OLS bridge; Tables 1–3 test final benchmark robustness; Figure 6/Table 5 test local and boundary detail; Table 4 tests derived shading quality; Table 6 removes or changes clamp, material augmentation, data, backbone, input, and light path.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: The supplied 13-page PDF has no appendix: p.11 begins REFERENCES after Discussion/Acknowledgment on p.10. Main text calls rendering/camera/augmentation details, benchmark image indices, additional qualitative analyses, and additional experiments an appendix, but no such objects are present in the PDF.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Nimbus Roman No9 L dominates body/caption/table text, Computer Modern handles equations, and Arial-like labels occur inside raster figures. Captions are about 9.963 pt, tables about 7 pt, and figure labels 5–14 pt; table/figure density makes the smallest text the common bottleneck.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Best/second table fills are consistent, but figure colors are local: normal directions, angular errors, dataset bars, light glyphs, and trainability colors are not globally interchangeable. Several visuals use saturated pseudo-color without grayscale or color-vision-safe alternatives.

most_reusable_patterns: Use a fixed-object normal/detail-crop/surface sequence (Figure 2) to turn appearance-versus-geometry failure into an observable mechanism, then quantify the representation difference (Figure 3).
Draw generated intermediate representations as an explicit input→conditioning→generator→intermediate→analytic solver→output chain, with freeze/train/physics legend (Figure 5).
Keep per-object columns beside aggregate Mean in benchmark and ablation tables, and add threshold coverage when robustness tails matter (Tables 1–3 and 6).
Align normal, error, ground truth/input, and a shared error colorbar in one qualitative grid (Figure 6), paired with selection rules and full-population summaries.
highest_value_objects: Figure 5: method interface and freeze/train/physics boundary.
Figure 2 plus Figure 3: tight visual failure-to-mechanism bridge.
failure_patterns: Point estimates omit spread, seeds, intervals, costs, and failure values across Tables 1–6 and Figures 1/3/6.
Pseudo-color normal/error maps are not grayscale-safe and use different semantics across figures.
Figure 4 shows six-light theory geometry while the text selects nine lights experimentally, without an explicit distinction in the figure.
Table 3 leaves objects-versus-2,800-samples denominator ambiguous; Figure 3/6 rely on a few selected objects.
The body points to an appendix that is absent; Table 4 derives other-method shading from predicted normals, so it is not a direct causal test of sequence generation.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: RoSE orders visual evidence as visible 3D misalignment → representation sensitivity → ring-light/OLS bridge → generation pipeline → benchmark/threshold/intermediate/detail results → broad ablations, achieving a compressed mechanism story through selected objects and point estimates while the promised appendix is absent.
